inline.s: Li Tangshi, whose given name was Siman, had lived for generations at Pingchao Township, Nantong, Jiangsu. Reared in the teachings of her family, she was by nature kind and gentle. In the hours between her household duties she would hold and recite the Buddha’s name. Though she had no fixed daily regimen, she was diligent and unremitting. Whenever a family member traveled afar or felt unwell, she would recite all the more earnestly. She was granted responses from time to time, but kept them secret and never spoke of them. In the spring of the wuyin year she fled the turmoil to Shanghai, where four years passed. Unused to the life of the city, her health declined daily; she soon fell into a deficiency of vital qi and returned to her hometown to recuperate, and gradually recovered. Yet as summer turned to autumn her illness worsened again, and Chinese and Western treatments alike proved of no avail. On the eleventh day of the tenth lunar month, at the hour of hai, she passed away quietly at the age of sixty-four. When she was critically ill her mind was clear and unobstructed: single-mindedly she recited the Buddha’s name and bade her family to chant in support of her. At the moment of death her left hand formed the Cundi mudra, and she was serene and free of pain. After the first of the tenth month she would ask those present, ‘Is it the eleventh today?’, as if she already knew when her hour would come. After she had passed, within two hours her son first saw a vapor rising from the crown of his mother’s head, spiraling gently upward, and then the whole family saw it as well.

Lady Guo, the mother of the layman Jiang Weinong, was by nature broad-minded, kind, thrifty, and respectful. She served her parents-in-law with filial devotion and helped her husband and raised her children, possessing much of the virtuous-mother bearing of ancient times. In daily life she wore no fine clothes and ate no delicacies; she liked to do everything by her own hand and never relied on others. In her later years she met with upheavals of the age and her family fortune was swept away, yet she remained at peace. She would often say, ‘All beings experience suffering; all dharmas are empty. What flourishes must fade, and what is born must die — this is the natural order. Whoever does not understand this and gives rise to vain sorrow or joy only adds to his suffering.’ From her youth Lady Guo revered Avalokiteshvara and regularly recited the Heart Sutra of Prajna. In her later years she began to keep a long-term vegetarian diet, and her chanting and worship grew ever more devout. Each day she recited the Heart Sutra seven times and the sacred name of Amitabha five thousand times. Whenever she was interrupted while reciting she would start again from the beginning, never willing to skim past it carelessly; her practice was meticulous for the most part. In the summer of 1921 her appetite suddenly failed, and she often spoke to the family of the impermanence of the defiled world. On the evening of the second day of the sixth month, seated cross-legged upon her bed, she closed her eyes, joined her palms, and said to the layman Weinong, ‘When I die, let it be just like this. Do you see that it is all right?’ In early June she drank only half a bowl of rice gruel each day and asked her son, the layman Weinong, to speak on the Amitabha Sutra; Weinong and his family took turns sitting and chanting the Buddha’s name beside her, and Lady Guo was greatly pleased. When she was sixty she had suffered from partial deafness, but now her hearing suddenly became acute, so that even a whisper in another room she could hear distinctly. On the morning of the fifteenth she said to the lay devotees chanting nearby, ‘The weather is hot; please rest a while, the hour is still early. I will not go until noon.’ At ten minutes past twelve she asked to be raised and seated, arranged her clothes and shoes herself, faced the West, joined her palms, and gazed up into the sky with a fixed smile; and so she passed away in peace. Her eyes were closed yet her smile could still be seen. She was eighty-two years old. After her passing her body was supple and her crown warm, and when she was encoffined the next day her complexion was rosy and full, like a person of some fifty years.

Madam Zhang was a native of Qingdao with one son and one daughter, and her family was poor. Her husband made his living pulling a cart at the harbor. Madam Zhang lived near the Zhanshan Hermitage in the city of Qingdao; within the hermitage there was a Buddhist Study Society, and on each Sunday Master Tanxu would come there to lecture on the sutras. Through this connection she took refuge in the Three Jewels and came to hear the Dharma. In the winter of the twenty-sixth year, one morning at dawn, she suddenly said to her husband, ‘Look after the children well. Today I shall be reborn in the Buddha-land.’ Her husband took it for a joke, made no answer, and went off to pull the cart at the dock. Madam Zhang then admonished her two sons, ‘Today I shall be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. You two must obey your father and not be mischievous.’ The boys were still young and did not understand; they went on playing as before. Madam Zhang tidied the household, then washed her face, combed her hair, changed into clean clothes, and sat cross-legged on the bed facing West; and reciting the Buddha’s name she passed on to rebirth. When her two sons returned to the room and saw that their mother had died, they ran weeping to the neighbors’ house to give word, and the neighbors hurried over and saw that Madam Zhang had been gone for some time. Her husband returned from the dock and wept bitterly; and because the family was too poor to prepare the coffin, the lay devotees of the Buddhist Study Society pooled their funds to settle her funeral affairs. Master Daguang recorded the matter thus.

Lu Liaoshun was a native of Wuxian County who lived in Yuejin Lane, Suzhou. She was born in 1911 outside Tuanzi Jing in Lijia Township. Her family had farmed for generations, planting in the busy season and reeling silk in the slack. At seventeen she married Lu Nianxiang, who worked in the silk-weaving trade. The lady was by nature kind and gentle, thrifty in managing her household, filial to her mother-in-law, and attentive to her husband. In November 1933, while working in the fields, she was blinded in one eye by the lime dust of a pigpen, and before long both eyes went dark; no treatment could cure them. Nianxiang reflected that his mother’s ailment had been cured through sincere recitation of Avalokiteshvara, and that only by reliance on the Buddha’s power could he hope to restore his wife’s sight. So he took his wife to pay respects to the Elder Yinguang and told him the whole matter. The elder said, ‘The Universal Gate chapter states: “Spotless pure light, the sun of wisdom breaks all darkness, stills the disasters of wind and fire, its universal brightness illumines the world.” So long as you sincerely invoke the sacred name of Avalokiteshvara, you will obtain a response.’ The lady followed the elder’s instruction, resolved to eat only vegetables, and earnestly chanted the bodhisattva’s name. After seven months of this, on the third day of the sixth lunar month — the festival of Weituo (Skanda) Bodhisattva — she happened to be staying at Ruyi Convent on Zhusi Lane. When she had finished the morning service and walked out of the great hall she suddenly felt a flash of light before her eyes; looking up she could make out the rows of roof-tiles, and the peach trees by the house, heavy with fruit, she now saw clearly as well. Overjoyed beyond measure, she knew that both her eyes had completely recovered. From then on she could thread a needle and manage every household task, just as before her illness; and afterwards she also learned the two daily services. On the first day of the ninth month of 1940 she knew beforehand the hour of her coming and said that three days later, at the hour of xu, she would pass on to rebirth. And when the time came she did, lying in a peaceful and auspicious manner, at the age of thirty-three.

Lu Liaokong was a native of Lijia, Wuxian County, Jiangsu. Her mother’s family was named Que, and she was born in the thirteenth year of the Guangxu reign of the Qing dynasty. Her family had been poor farmers and lived in Yuejin Lane, Suzhou. When she was some thirty-five or thirty-six she was suddenly stricken with gout; her hands and feet contracted and could not move, and hospital treatment proved entirely without effect. Her son Lu Nianxiang, a devoted Buddhist, was able to show her filial love, and seeing his mother’s incurable illness he was greatly distressed. When the lady was forty-nine her son Nianxiang supported her to the Baoguo Monastery on Chuanxin Street, where she took refuge with the Elder Yinguang. Moved by the master’s compassionate acceptance, she was enrolled as a disciple and given the name Liaokong; Nianxiang too took refuge at the same time and was given the name Liaozhong. The elder instructed the mother and son to sincerely invoke the sacred name of Avalokiteshvara, and that in time they would surely obtain a response. After returning home the mother and son reverently followed the teacher’s instruction and ceaselessly chanted the bodhisattva’s name; and seeking his mother’s early recovery, Nianxiang cut his own arm to heal her. After nine months her illness was indeed cured, and her hands and feet could bend and stretch once more, no different from before. At fifty-six, in the renwu year of 1942, on the twenty-ninth day of the ninth lunar month, she passed away without illness. Two days before her passing she said to her son Nianxiang, ‘In two more days I shall go to the West; you must help me recite the Buddha’s name with all your heart and see me off to rebirth.’ Nianxiang did as she bade and chanted the sacred name for her, and his mother likewise chanted with utmost sincerity, the sound of the Buddha’s name unbroken; and indeed on the twenty-ninth she sat and passed away in peace.

The mother of the venerable layman Fei Fanjiu of Nantong was named Li Gui. She was a native of Nantong and lived in Pingchao Township of that county. At seventeen she married Fei Jianqing, the father of the layman Fanjiu. She managed the household with thrift and good order; and after her husband died she took refuge in Buddhism and recited the sacred name of Avalokiteshvara daily, never once ceasing even when illness and pain came upon her. Whatever the household trifles, she did herself and never employed servants. Her house had ample ground, and she turned it into a vegetable plot, planting and watering and weeding it herself and finding joy in this; around the plot she planted fruit trees everywhere. She would say, ‘Even an inch of ground should not be left waste.’ Wherever she saw a living creature on the land she forbade people to tread on it; and fruit and melons she would not let be picked until they were ripe, and once picked she first offered them to the Buddha and her ancestors before sharing them with the family. In 1938 she fled the turmoil to Shanghai, where her lodging was cramped and mean; and in the winter of 1941 she returned to her old home in Nantong. After her return she fell ill in the tenth month, and after five months of sickness passed away. Throughout her illness her mind remained extraordinarily clear. Three days before her passing she dreamed of wandering to a place where she saw majestic halls and countless jeweled trees, and she saw a lotus flower as large as a peck measure, fresh and red and lovely. When she woke she told her family, ‘Ever since I have seen this flower I no longer hold you all in my heart.’ Eight hours after her death the crown of her head was still warm. Mother Fei was born in the ninth year of the Tongzhi reign of the Qing dynasty and died in the third month of 1943, at the age of seventy-four.

Chui Yuxian was from East Street, Fufeng County, Shaanxi. She took refuge with Master Liangqing at Famen Monastery and embraced the Pure Land teaching. With faith and vow she recited the Buddha’s name, and within less than three years she passed on to rebirth. Her son Ran Hengtong, a pure-hearted devotee, urged his mother to embrace the Buddha; but as she was old the mother feared she could make no attainment and could not decide. When she went to Famen Monastery to pay respects to Master Liangqing, the master knew her concern and encouraged her: ‘In the practice of Buddha-recitation there is neither old nor young; only see that you are utterly sincere, and you are sure to succeed.’ He then recounted several stories from the ancients of attaining rebirth through ten recitations. The lady believed without doubt, made her vow, and practiced diligently, never ceasing to recite. On an evening in the autumn of 1953, while she sat in a dark cave dwelling, she suddenly saw the Three Holy Ones of the West seated high above. Forgetting that she was in the dark cave, she said in great joy, ‘I have chanted the Buddha’s name so long, and only today do I see you, venerable ones.’ Before she had finished speaking the images vanished and the cave was dark again as before. The next day she asked the master about it, and the master cautioned her not to give rise to a mind of joy. When she went home she recited with even greater effort: in doing her household chores, one pull of the bellows and one recitation, one stroke of the broom and one recitation, one cut of the knife and one recitation, one turn of the spinning wheel and one recitation — and even walking along carrying a child, she never ceased silently invoking the sacred name. In the spring of 1954, on the evening of the third day of the third month, while she was performing the evening service in the cave, she suddenly saw a radiance shining through the cave, dazzling and bright. At first she thought the grandchildren were playing with fire and went to stop them; but when she stepped outside she saw the Three Holy Ones hovering in the sky, and she at once knelt and bowed. She heard Avalokiteshvara say, ‘On the morning of the eleventh I shall come to receive you.’ Knowing her hour of rebirth had come, she hastily settled her affairs, told her family to prepare a bed and seat, and had her son Hengtong take out the clothes for the dead. On the evening of the tenth of the third month, Master Liangqing came with the masters Huiming and Shaoguang and the layman Li Bingbo to assist the recitation; and on the morning of the eleventh she ended her life without illness, at eighty-three. Three hours later her crown was still warm; she sat upright and straight for a whole day and night as if still alive. The incense burned in the cave was ordinary, yet everyone smelled the fragrance of sandalwood and orchids pervading the whole room, and all held it to be extraordinary.

Mei Zhongfu was the mother of the layman Shi Chunfu. She was illiterate. She took refuge with the Venerable Master Xuyun and was given the Dharma name Kuanyi. In 1945, at seventy-one, her son Chunfu brought her to his residence in Tianjin to care for her. Chunfu was a pure-hearted devotee and had long since received the refuge and precepts from Master Cizhou. After his mother arrived in Tianjin, Chunfu urged her to eat only vegetables and recite the Buddha’s name, seeking rebirth in the Pure Land; the mother answered vaguely, still hesitant in mind. One night she dreamed of an old woman in white, tall and graceful, of very solemn bearing, holding a vase in her left hand and a long object in her right, coming slowly and calmly. The next morning she asked her son about it; the son showed her the sacred image of the White-robed Mahasattva, and his mother said, ‘It is she!’ From then on she kept a long-term vegetarian diet and recited the Buddha’s name, never relenting in her constant practice. Later Chunfu established a Buddhist scriptures distribution center in Hong Kong, and in 1957 his mother was eighty-three. At year’s end Chunfu came back from Hong Kong to visit. She was suffering from cataracts and had been blind for a long time. She said to her son, ‘These past year or two I sit facing the wall. Time and again I see a broad open road, very distant; at the end of the road there is a great monastery, supremely majestic. On the road men and women, old and young, all in ancient dress, are walking calmly toward the monastery. What I see is extraordinarily clear; I often gaze on it for hours, until my eyes are quite tired before I stop.’ She also said, ‘I often dream of a great monastery, resplendent and magnificent beyond words, with Amitabha Buddha seated in the midst of the hall.’ In the months before she gave up her body she had such dreams again and again. A few days before her passing she said to her daughter-in-law, ‘I have myself seen the sublime and marvelous land of Ultimate Bliss. I tell you now so that you will record it carefully and show it to Chunfu when he returns to Tianjin.’ She also instructed, ‘Write quickly to Chunfu and tell him to get home before the seventeenth of the eleventh month, to see me off to rebirth.’ Chunfu received the news and hastened back to Tianjin, but his mother had already passed six hours before; and when he saw what his wife had recorded, and that it matched the descriptions in the Pure Land scriptures, he was all the more amazed. His mother passed away at two in the morning of a winter month in 1958. At the moment of her death her daughter-in-law was keeping watch in the room; through a haze she heard the sound of flutes and drums and music outside the bedroom, and heard someone say, ‘It is this very house.’ Suddenly a gust of wind blew the door open and she awoke with a start: the mother had already ceased to breathe. Three days later, when she was encoffined, her whole body was soft as in life.

Chen Deyi was from Suzhou; her husband’s family name was Ni. Both her father’s family and her husband’s family were chiefly silk merchants. After marriage the couple were not in harmony, yet they had one son and one daughter. In middle age she came to feel deeply the emptiness of life and that wealth and honor could never long be kept, and so by degrees she grew in faith toward the Dharma. In 1931 she went to Lingyan and took refuge with the Elder Yinguang, who gave her the name Deyi. In her daily practice she knew only to recite the Buddha’s name wholeheartedly and studied no other methods; she revered the Three Jewels and delighted in giving to others. In 1962, at seventy-two, feeling unwell, she set her mind single-mindedly on seeking rebirth in the West. At the end, amid the gathered Dharma friends reciting the sacred name in support, she was still able to join them in chanting; with clear right mindfulness she passed away peacefully.

Chen Zhiqi was from Suzhou, known to all as Old Madam Chen, and lived at No. 1 in front of the Wenshan Temple in Suzhou. She had taken refuge with Master Yinguang and received the Dharma name Zhiqi; later she also took refuge with the Venerable Master Xuyun and received the name Kuanrong. The old lady had root conditions from a former life; from childhood she had known to follow her mother in reciting the Buddha’s name. In middle age her husband died, and having no children she lived very poor. By nature gentle, she could endure any hardship, loved to help others, and never stinted even in her own straitened circumstances. Every day she recited the Surangama Mantra, the Great Compassion Mantra, the Universal Gate chapter, the Diamond Sutra, and the Amitabha and other Mahayana scriptures, never once interrupting. The old lady knew well that birth and death are great matters; she practiced repentance with vigor and recited the Buddha’s name with a single mind, vowing to attain rebirth. On the twenty-sixth of March, 1974, around ten in the morning, a fellow devotee came bringing vegetables and pushed open the door. The old lady said, ‘You have come just in time; please help me wipe my body and change into clean clothes.’ At this her friend understood at once and urged her to recite the Buddha’s name. The old lady said, ‘There is no need for many words; I already know my hour has come.’ Then she burned incense before the Buddha and sat down, and sang out, ‘Cast the refuse to the East; I go now to the West.’ Having said this she passed away smiling, at the age of eighty-two.

Zhu Huiying was from Dongshan, Suzhou, and kept her chastity without marrying. From the womb she had been a vegetarian: when her mother made her eat meat she firmly refused, and her mother could not force her. She took refuge with Master Desen and practiced the Pure Land path. She was extremely poor, and her younger sister and brother-in-law gave her constant support. In 1976 she fell ill with stomach bleeding. A few days before death she saw two small children beating her legs, and wherever they struck there were bruises; knowing this was the effect of past karma, she recited the Buddha’s name with a single mind, and the apparitions disappeared. As she was about to die she saw the Buddha come, and said she must see the lotus flower before going; in a short time the lotus appeared in the empty sky, and only then did she pass away. By her last instruction her ashes were mixed with flour into balls and cast into the sea.

Xu Liaofa was a native of Wuxi, Jiangsu, residing at No. 11 Yuqing Lane on Yunnan South Road, Shanghai. She had embraced Buddhism in her youth, and in middle age her husband died; having no children, she was quite alone. The lady had great zeal for spreading the Dharma and benefiting living beings. She led a society of fellow practitioners and with devout mind recited the Buddha’s name, and had made pilgrimage to famous mountains and monasteries in many places. Whenever the monastic community, or laypersons who were struggling, needed aid, she would come at once; and in tending the sick and chanting for the dying she did her utmost, sparing no toil. Her strength was very weak, and later she suddenly contracted breast cancer, yet of her own accord and heedless of danger she still tended the illnesses of others without any sign of weariness. Poor in worldly means, she lived by selling off her clothes and never asked anyone for help; and if anyone gave her goods or money she would sincerely dedicate the merit before the Buddha. Before her passing her home had nothing left on its four walls but a wooden cabinet she used for offerings. By then the breast cancer had reached its late stage, and since she also suffered from other illnesses she could not undergo surgery; knowing that medicine could no longer save her, she earnestly prayed before the image of Avalokiteshvara, seeking rebirth in the Pure Land. Though the diseased part had ulcerated and pus and blood flowed, she felt no pain. On the first day of the seventh lunar month of 1977, at eleven in the morning, she passed on to rebirth. She had known her hour beforehand and said that on the first of the seventh month she would go. When that day came, past eight in the morning, after she had eaten some watermelon she said to those attending her, ‘Make haste and burn incense for me — the Mahasattva’s coming has arrived.’ She asked to be raised, joined her palms, and made a bow toward the south window, invoking the sacred name of the Mahasattva. After a moment she lay down again, and those attending her all chanted the sacred name intently. The lady said, ‘Please lower your voices and recite more slowly, or I shall not be able to keep up.’ The neighbors on either side all came to look; her lips moved slightly, and her countenance was as usual. They said among themselves, ‘Old Madam Xu is still reciting.’ Little did they know that the lady had already, amid the sound of recitation, passed on to rebirth in peace. She was seventy-one.

Li Huiguang was from Suzhou, Jiangsu, living at No. 4 Hexiadang in Suzhou; her husband’s family name was Song. She bore one son, who died just at twenty. Grieving deeply over the impermanence of the defiled world and the manifold sufferings of life, she kept a long-term vegetarian diet and embraced the Buddha, taking refuge with Master Yuanying of the Yuanming Lecture Hall in Shanghai, who gave her the Dharma name Huiguang. Later she also took refuge with the Tiantai master Venerable Jingquan, and with the Suzhou bhiksuni Runtian. In her life the lady delighted in charity and was especially reverent toward the monastic community. Each day, besides the morning and evening services, she recited the Lotus Sutra, and for several decades never once missed a day. In her later years her circumstances were poor and her health failing, but she never stopped reciting the Buddha’s name. She was used to hardship and endurance, and when she saved a little from her household expenses she would give it to those she saw in poverty. A few days before the Spring Festival of 1959 she felt slightly unwell. On the morning of New Year’s Day, Nun Runtian came to visit; the lady said, ‘Please place some fruit as an offering before the Buddha’s image.’ And she added, ‘When I pass on, it is best that no one be by my side, so as not to disturb me; I shall recite the Buddha’s name myself.’ On the second day of the new year, at eleven o’clock and five minutes, she passed on to rebirth. A moment before she said to those attending her, ‘Please light a stick of incense for me before the Buddha.’ And having spoken, she lay still and silent; when they looked, she was gone. After she passed, the Dharma friends gathered and recited the Buddha’s name, and for five days and nights the sound of recitation did not stop. When she was carried to the cremation her complexion was rosy and her face wore a smile. By her last instruction her ashes were made into balls and cast into the pond of releasing life at the Western Garden, thereby forming a bond with the water-dwellers. She was eighty-two.

Yang Chenian was from Xizuo Village, Fufeng County, Shaanxi; her husband’s family name was Zhao. At twenty-four she lost her husband and resolved to keep her chastity and filial virtue in the Zhao household. She served her in-laws well and did her utmost in filial devotion, raising her husband’s brother’s children as her own. She lived in harmony with her sisters-in-law, restrained herself, bore labor without complaint, and dealt with relatives, friends, and neighbors with gentleness and courtesy, never contending; everyone called her virtuous and kind. By nature she loved quietness and delighted in performing good deeds. She took refuge with Master Liangqing, who taught her the Pure Land practice; and so she kept a long-term vegetarian diet and recited the Buddha’s name, hoping to be reborn in the Pure Land. She practiced diligently, never relaxing by day or night, for more than thirty years. In November 1980 she took to her bed; although she could no longer kneel and bow or chant, she still sat in stillness cultivating contemplation. In the first ten days of the twelfth month her long illness gradually healed, and she resumed bowing and chanting as usual. But she said to her family, ‘Do not think my illness is mending — without fail I shall go West in the first month.’ Since her limbs were light and easy, the family did not pay much attention. Her nephew’s wife, Li Fengxia, who had root conditions from a former life and loved her aunt dearly, invited monks to hold a seven-day retreat in prayer that the aunt’s calamities be dispelled and her life extended. On New Year’s Eve the altar was purified and the session began, the four assemblies gathering. The lady alone tidied her clothes and her stores, giving them away to relatives, friends, and the monks, and asked them to assist in chanting for her at death; moved, they all consented. On the night of the fifth of the first month of the next year, around eleven o’clock, the lady suddenly asked the group to rest, and said that at six the next morning she would surely go West; the more earnestly they chanted. The next day, exactly when the clock pointed to six, she sat upright and straight, and amid the sound of the Buddha’s name passed away in calm. She was seventy-six. Three hours later the top of her head was still warm, her limbs were supple, and her bearing was serene, as in life. After her passing some of the family dreamed of a man affixing a certificate of merit to the door, and some dreamed of a man offering five-colored flowers before her portrait.

Tang Quennlang, whose Dharma name was Jingxiu, lived in Zhangjia Residence, north of Chengqiao on Chongming Island, Shanghai, and made her living spinning yarn. After marriage she bore no children of her own and adopted a son and a daughter. When the son grew up he was of a vicious temper, showed her no filial devotion, and tormented her in every way. Tang had taken refuge in the Three Jewels and devoutly practiced, never once skipping the morning and evening services. During the Cultural Revolution religious policy was destroyed, and this son repeatedly snatched away his mother’s prayer books and beads, handing them to the rebel faction as evidence of guilt, so that she suffered great persecution. Having taken vows to refrain from killing and to eat only vegetables, she was yet forced by this son to eat meat. Unable to bear the abuse, she once left home and entered a home for the aged; but since it was inconvenient to keep a vegetarian diet there, she returned home. In her extreme suffering she once contemplated suicide. Someone counseled her, ‘A disciple of the Buddha should not take his own life; one who kills himself must be full of hatred and countless other afflictions and loses the right mindfulness of Buddha-recitation. Not only will he fail to be reborn in the Pure Land, but he will fall into evil destinies. You must endure with boundless patience, keep reciting the Buddha’s name, and seek rebirth in the Pure Land.’ Tang heeded these words and accepted what came with resignation; in her harsh circumstances her faith grew all the firmer, her longing for the Pure Land and renunciation of the world became all the more earnest, and her vegetarianism and recitation became all the more vigorous. On the fourteenth day of the third lunar month of 1981 she was still in good health at lunch, but by evening her daughter discovered that Tang had already sat and passed away in a small room. What was especially remarkable: the seat had no backrest, yet Tang sat upright and straight, her countenance as if alive. She was seventy-eight.

Wu Zhengguo was the third daughter of Mr. Wu Baohe of Yanling. At twenty-one she married into the Du household. Being too poor for a home of her own, she lodged in the Wu household of the same village; and she was content there, never once repining in the least because she had been born into wealth. Though she lived in poverty, she disciplined herself in hardship, diligent and thrifty, saving up her earnings little by little; and after more than ten years she finally built herself a house. When she moved, her landlord, unable to part with her, wept as he saw her off, and she wept too. Ever afterwards, at every festival she would prepare gifts to show her regard, never forgetting the kindness of having been lodged there. Throughout her life the lady was upright, kind-hearted, of humble and gentle disposition, hardworking and thrifty, and glad to help and give. She was filial to her mother-in-law, strict in raising her son, and gracious with her neighbors, so that she was praised throughout the village. From childhood she had revered the Three Jewels, and from age forty she kept a long-term vegetarian diet. At sixty-eight she followed her son Taifeng to Jiangpu and settled at Dufeng, where she formally took refuge in the Three Jewels and received the Dharma name Zhengguo. From then on she was resolved and never stepped beyond the door; apart from her daily work she had only Amitabha in mind. Past ninety she was still as clear-minded as anyone, and at ninety-four she even grew three new teeth, a thing indeed strange. On the tenth of January 1985, catching a slight cold, at seven in the evening she felt mildly unwell; in a while she recovered and lay on her left side. At half-past eleven in the night, in the stillness when all sounds were hushed, amid the recitation in support of her, she passed away in peace. The next day, when they changed her clothes, her limbs were supple, her lips and cheeks rosy, and her face as in life: her eyes closed, her mouth shut, as if in sleep. On the third day she was placed in the jar, and on the seventh day, when the round was completed, the funeral pyre was lit. From the cremation were obtained five-colored relic flowers: over twenty green ones, some ten yellow, a few pieces of a green hue, some ten red, and one white one as large as a jujube. All who saw them marveled, and those who knew declared this was proof of her rebirth. The lady was born on the fifteenth of the second month of 1890 and lived ninety-four years. Master Yuanche composed a verse in praise:
A hundred years, a finger-snap, and all is gone; the sudden news of death was ever well foreknown.
Blest that in this very life she attained release — her jewel-relic flowers now bless the unknowing many.

The mother of the layman Cai Chu’ang was from Zhenjiang, Jiangsu. She was virtuous and refined and lived a hard, simple life. The layman Chu’ang lost his father at thirteen; his mother kept her widowhood and raised her orphan, teaching her son to become a man. The layman served his mother with the utmost filial devotion: whenever she was displeased he would kneel long before her until her heart was happy again before rising. Mother Cai originally knew nothing of Buddhism. At sixty-five, through Chu’ang’s earnest persuasion and his explaining the general meaning of the Dharma, she began to believe and to recite the Buddha’s name. At seventy-two she suddenly fell ill, took to her bed for nearly ten days and nights, and ate very little. Chu’ang invited many Dharma friends for his mother, who took turns chanting for ten days and nights. On the ninth day Mother Cai suddenly opened her eyes and said, ‘Tomorrow at noon I shall pass on to rebirth in the West.’ And indeed at noon the next day, chanting the Buddha’s name in peace, she passed away. More than ten hours after her death the top of her head was still warm.

Old Madam Wu of Shanghai lived in the lane beside the Buddhist Study Society on Changzhi Road. By nature kind, she kept a long-term vegetarian diet and recited the Buddha’s name. Three years before her death she learned to recite the Lotus Sutra, one scroll a day, and at other times she would recite the Buddha’s name. Later she suffered from a back ailment and could not leave her bed, yet she never ceased her sutra-chanting and recitation. Her husband and daughter did not believe in Buddhism and mocked her as deluded. At the time of her death her husband and daughter were at her side when they suddenly saw Avalokiteshvara appear — now the whole body, now half the body. Filled with joy and wonder, they all knelt and bowed. The old lady saw them and said, ‘So today you too believe!’ Having said this she closed her eyes and passed away.

Han Yeshi was the wife of the layman Han Huazhong, president of the Shaoxing Buddhist Study Society of Zhejiang. She was originally from Xiaoshan. In her thirties she began to keep a vegetarian diet and serve the Buddha. At forty she journeyed to Putuo of the South Sea and took refuge with Master Jingwu of Fayu Monastery, receiving also the Five Precepts and the Eight Precepts of fasting. She made pilgrimage to Putuo five times in all, and also made pilgrimage to the Guoqing Temple at Tiantai. She joined the Shaoxing Buddhist Study Society and went often to recite the Buddha’s name. Seven days before her death she dreamed of a bodhisattva whose fingers emitted light, and within the light appeared the image of Amitabha Buddha; and seven days later, joining her palms and sitting cross-legged, she passed away reciting the Buddha’s name. She was fifty-seven.

The layman Xiao Houzhai of Hangzhou had a daughter, whose name is forgotten. When the girl was born, her mother dreamed of an old woman holding a baby and giving it to her, and telling her it was a girl. As she grew she was extraordinarily clever, loved to handle brush and ink, and delighted in sketching and painting. She had great faith in Buddhism and was very diligent in revering the Buddha and reciting the sutras. At twenty-one she suddenly fell ill, and long treatment could not cure her. In that same year, on the nineteenth day of the second lunar month — the festival of Avalokiteshvara — she passed on to rebirth. After her death a strange fragrance filled the room and did not waft away for days.

The daughter of the layman Chen Yiren, whose name is forgotten, kept a long-term vegetarian diet from childhood and knew the path of Buddha-recitation. At nineteen she knew of herself that her hour of rebirth had come, and her mother invited many Pure Land friends to chant the Buddha’s name and see her off to rebirth. The girl then said, ‘I have already seen Amitabha Buddha, seated upright with palms joined, ready to pass into stillness.’ Among those chanting there was a bhiksuni who repeatedly stroked the girl’s head with her hand and had her mother place silver in the girl’s mouth, this being the custom of the time. Her mother was chanting and waved her hand to decline, but the nun went on chattering endlessly. At that the girl suddenly cried out sternly, ‘My going to the West is ruined! It is all this nun’s doing. I had seen the Buddha come to welcome me, and I grasped the sleeve of the Buddha’s robe with my right hand and was rising into the sky toward the West. Though I had gone with the Buddha, I could hear your recitations and all your actions with perfect clarity. This nun touched my head with her hand and told my mother to put silver in my mouth; the moment I heard it I was displeased, and before I knew it the thought stirred, and Amitabha Buddha vanished.’ Her father, the layman Chen Yiren, hearing this, said, ‘This is a great pity indeed, but it is no obstacle. You have the merit of years of practice. Make haste and diligently keep the sacred name, and you will surely attain rebirth as you wish.’ The girl heard her father’s words, repented wholeheartedly, and continued chanting the Buddha’s name for seven days. When the seven-day session was complete she once again saw Amitabha Buddha appear before her; then she sat upright, joined her palms, and amid the sound of recitation passed away with a smile.
